name: npm_upgrade_planner_agent
description: An agent that audits a project's npm dependencies with the POST_scan tool exposed through the Orkes MCP Gateway (the scan_npm_package workflow), then writes an upgrade plan. The LLM chooses each scan; the workflow allowlists the tool, checks every call before it runs (no repeats, no finishing before every dependency is scanned), caps the loop at 10 steps, and keeps a ledger of every result. POST_assess is not used: an assessment can take over a minute, and the gateway cuts calls off at about 60 seconds. Its only write is optional: version 2 posts the finished plan as a GitHub issue, in the repo named by the environment variables dependency_review_github_owner and dependency_review_github_repo. Before saving: create the secret dependency_tools_key holding the MCP Gateway API key; the GitHub step uses the main workflow's secret and environment variables.

inputParameters.queryExpression:
# prepare_agent_context: keeps only the allowed tools, and turns the inputs into text for the prompt.
# allowedToolNames are the names the MCP Gateway gives the routes the agent may use (POST_scan).
# POST_assess is left out: an assessment can take over a minute, and the gateway cuts calls off at
# about 60 seconds.
.allowedToolNames as $allowed
| [ (.tools // [])[] | select(.name as $n | any($allowed[]; . == $n)) | {name, description, inputSchema} ] as $tools
| {
    allowedTools: [ $tools[].name ],
    toolsText: ($tools | tojson),
    dependenciesText: (.dependencies | tojson),
    # Allowed tools the server didn't list, e.g. a renamed route. The planner can't call them.
    missingTools: [ $allowed[] | . as $n | select(any($tools[]; .name == $n) == false) ]
  }

tasks.name: agent_loop

messages.message:
You plan dependency upgrades for an npm project. You can call a scan tool that checks one exact npm package version at a time. It returns security facts: the package's own advisories with their severity and fixed versions, an upgrade target (recommendedVersion), and the advisories across its dependency tree, each with the version that fixes it.

Work toward the goal one step at a time. Each turn, choose exactly one action:
- call_tool: check one package version. Use only the tools listed. Use exact versions such as 4.17.1, never ranges such as ^4.17.1, and never 'latest'.
- finish: when the results are enough to write the plan, or nothing useful is left to check.

Rules:
- You have at most 10 steps in total, and each call uses one. Plan for them.
- Scan every current dependency first. The workflow won't let you finish until each one has been scanned.
- For a package already in the project, use only its current version or a version that appears in a result (a recommendedVersion or a fixedIn). Never guess a version number.
- A result with a "warning" means the tool had no data for that version: it may not exist. Treat it like a failed call, never as clean.
- Before recommending a version, scan it. If it still has HIGH or CRITICAL advisories in its dependencies, you may scan one newer version from a result.
- If a package is deprecated or rejected, or its own advisory has no fixed version, you may check one replacement package. Start that call's reason with "Replacement for <package>:", e.g. "Replacement for request: scan node-fetch 3.2.10". Only use a version you saw in an earlier result or are sure exists; if its scan comes back with a warning, the version may not exist.
- If a call fails (its result has an "error"), don't retry it or look for another way to get the same result. Carry on with the results you have; the plan will list the failure.
- Never repeat a call that is already in the results: the workflow skips repeats, and they still use up a step.

Respond with JSON only, in exactly this shape:
{"action": "call_tool or finish", "tool": "the tool name, or empty when finishing", "arguments": {"packageName": "", "packageVersion": ""}, "reason": "one sentence"}

You write a dependency upgrade plan for an engineering team, from the ledger of an agent's tool calls. Use only facts from the ledger: never invent versions, advisories or verdicts. Write markdown with:
1. A one-paragraph summary.
2. A table with one row per current dependency: package, current version, what was found, the recommended action (keep, upgrade to a checked version, or replace with a checked package), and the evidence: the step numbers and their key facts.
   - In "what was found", count the package's own advisories and its dependencies' advisories separately, e.g. "2 own advisories (1 HIGH); 12 in dependencies (5 HIGH)".
   - For every package, whether you recommend keeping, upgrading or replacing it: if the version you recommend still has HIGH or CRITICAL advisories in its dependencies, put the npm overrides in the recommended action itself, naming each dependency's fixed version from the ledger, e.g. "upgrade to 4.20.0 and override path-to-regexp to 0.1.13" or "keep 5.58.0 and override dompurify to 3.4.17". A HIGH or CRITICAL dependency advisory with no fixed version is an unresolved risk: name it.
   - A package checked as a replacement (its reason starts "Replacement for <package>:") goes in the row of the package it replaces, not in a row of its own. Recommend it there if its checked version has no HIGH or CRITICAL advisories, and note that switching to a different package needs code changes.
   - Never recommend keeping a package whose own advisory has no fixed version without naming that as a risk. If the ledger has a checked replacement for it, recommend the replacement.
   - Never recommend a version if any call for it has an "error" or a "warning": list it under open questions as unverified. A warning means the version may not exist.
   - A current dependency with no scan in the ledger is "not checked": say so, and never recommend keeping it.
3. Open questions: anything the agent couldn't check, failed or skipped calls, and recommendations that weren't verified with a tool.
In the summary, say plainly whether the recommendations reach the goal, including any overrides they need. The goal is reached only if no HIGH or CRITICAL advisory remains in any package after the recommended actions; an unchecked package or an unresolved risk means it isn't. If a recommended version still has HIGH or CRITICAL advisories, of its own or in its dependencies, say so; never describe such a version as having "no advisories".
Never recommend a version or replacement that the ledger doesn't show as checked. Keep the plan under 500 words, and finish every section.

body.title: npm upgrade plan (agent run ${workflow.workflowId})
